hints: Look at the hair-like fringe along the top edge of the cells - think about which side air and mucus would move over as air flows through the airway.
walkthrough:
Picture which way up the lining sits**
Think of the bronchus as a tube. The wall is at the bottom of the photo and the hollow air space is at the top. Epithelial cells sit on the wall with their free surface facing the air.

Use the cilia as your compass**
Cilia always project from the free apical surface into the lumen so they can sweep mucus. In Fig. 1.1 the fuzzy fringe is at the top, so the lumen must be the empty area just above that fringe.
Final answer: X placed in the clear space above the cilia at the top of Fig. 1.1.

hints: Focus on the row of dark, oval bodies near the base of the cells - recall which large organelle stains darkly because it contains dense DNA.
walkthrough:
Read what A is pointing to**
The label line ends on one of the dark oval structures sitting in a row near the base of the epithelial layer. They are all similar in size and position in each cell.

Link dark staining to DNA**
In a stained light micrograph the nucleus looks dark because chromatin takes up stain strongly. That size, shape and basal position fits a nucleus, not a small organelle like a mitochondrion.

hints: Compare the shape of these tall cells and their top surface with what you know an alveolus needs - a very thin, flat wall for rapid diffusion with no need to move mucus.
walkthrough:
Recall the alveolus design**
Alveoli are lined by very thin, flat squamous cells with flattened nuclei to give the shortest possible diffusion distance for oxygen and carbon dioxide. They have no cilia and no mucus-secreting goblet cells.

Spot the opposite in Fig. 1.1**
Here you can clearly see a fuzzy border of cilia on top, tall columnar-shaped cells, rounded nuclei, and paler goblet cells between them. Any one of those visible features proves this cannot be thin alveolar lining.
Final answer: Presence of cilia on free surface / cells are columnar and tall / nuclei are rounded not flat / presence of goblet cells.

hints: Think about what kind of division must make more of the same diploid body cell for repair, rather than making haploid gametes with variation.
walkthrough:
Match division to job**
Replacing damaged lining cells needs genetically identical diploid cells with no reduction in chromosome number and no variation. That is the role of mitosis in growth and tissue repair.

Rule out meiosis**
Meiosis makes haploid gametes and creates variation, which would not help maintain a uniform protective epithelium. So the repair division is mitosis followed by cell growth and differentiation.

hints: Start from Fig. 1.1 as the healthy baseline - tall ciliated cells with normal mucus - and think about which two structures smoke irritates first.
Think about how repeated damage and repair changes cell shape and differentiation, and what builds up when the mucus escalator stops working.
Picture what a long-term irritated lining looks like under the microscope - cell height, surface hairs, mucus amount, and any deposits or defence cells.
walkthrough:
Start with loss of the mucus escalator**
Chemicals and heat in smoke paralyse and then destroy cilia, so you see shorter, fewer or missing cilia. At the same time goblet cells enlarge and secrete excess mucus, which then accumulates because it cannot be swept away.

Explain the change in cell type**
Chronic irritation and repeated repair leads to abnormal differentiation. Tall columnar ciliated cells are replaced by undifferentiated cells and then by flattened squamous cells, with scar tissue forming in the wall. This is squamous metaplasia.

Add the signs of irritation and defence**
You would also describe black tar deposits coating the lining, presence of phagocytes cleaning up debris, and inflammation of the bronchial lining. Any three distinct visible changes earn full credit, so give three separate points.

Final answer: Any three of: cilia shorter / fewer / absent / damaged / paralysed; undifferentiated cells present; cells become flattened squamous epithelium; scar tissue forms; enlarged goblet cells; excess accumulated mucus; tar deposits on lining; phagocytes present; inflammation of bronchial lining.
